concepts.definition: A separate chip that counts seconds with its own crystal and keeps the date; the Arduino asks it over I2C.
concepts.example: Your data logger writes a real time such as "2026-03-14 08:30:10" next to each measurement.
concepts.pitfall: Trying to keep the time with millis(); millis() resets when the power is cut, the RTC keeps going.

concepts.definition: rtc.now() gives the current time as a DateTime object; you get its parts with year(), month(), day(), hour(), minute(), second().
concepts.example: t.hour() returns 7; to show 07 on the screen, you add the leading zero yourself.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking month() comes back with two digits; for month 3 it returns 3, not "03".

concepts.definition: adjust() sets the time; lostPower() tells you whether the clock has stopped.
concepts.example: if (rtc.lostPower()) { rtc.adjust(DateTime(F(__DATE__), F(__TIME__))); } sets the time only when needed.
concepts.pitfall: Putting the adjust(__DATE__, __TIME__) line in setup() without a condition; every time the board switches on, the time goes back to the moment of compiling.

concepts.definition: The RTC module's name on the I2C line; there cannot be two devices with the same address on the line.
concepts.example: The RTC (0x68) and an I2C LCD (0x27) can share the same SDA and SCL wires.
concepts.pitfall: Connecting the MPU6050 and the RTC on the same line; both use 0x68 and they clash.

concepts.definition: A small battery in a real RTC module that keeps the clock running when the main power is cut.
concepts.example: With the battery fitted, if you unplug it and plug it back in an hour later, the time has moved on correctly.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the time stays right when the battery is flat; when the power is cut, the time is forgotten and has to be set again.

concepts.definition: The alarm condition stays true for a whole minute; a "has it gone off today?" variable makes the alarm go off once.
concepts.example: The sonTetikGunu variable keeps the day of the month on which the alarm last went off.
concepts.pitfall: Without a flag, restarting the alarm over and over during 07:30.

quiz.prompt: Why is an RTC used instead of millis() so that a device can answer the question "what time was it yesterday?" even days later?
options: millis() starts from zero when the board switches on and is forgotten when the power is cut; the RTC keeps the real date and time
The RTC always measures more precisely
quiz.explanation: millis() counts the time since the board switched on and resets at every restart. The RTC is a separate chip; it keeps the real date and time. Precision is not the real difference: millis() counts milliseconds, and there is no speed problem.

3 seconds after 23:59:58 the time is 00:00:01, and the year moves to 2027 and the date to 1 January. The RTC knows the calendar itself, so a value such as 2026-12-34 never comes out. month() and day() return numbers and do not add a leading zero; the output is 2027-1-1. To print 2027-01-01 you need two-digit formatting.

options: The rtc.adjust(...) line, because it runs without a condition; it should only be called if rtc.lostPower() is true
quiz.explanation: Because the adjust line has no condition, every time the board switches on it pulls the time back to the moment of compiling; the RTC's job of keeping the time when the power is cut is wasted. The fix: if (rtc.lostPower()) { ... }. Serial.begin and rtc.begin do not change the time value.

quiz.prompt: The alarm program sets the clock to 07:29:55. The alarm goes off at 07:30 and ALARM_SURESI lasts 5000 ms. About how many seconds after the program starts does the LED go off?
quiz.explanation: There are 5 seconds to go until the alarm time (from 07:29:55 to 07:30:00). After it goes off, it stays lit for 5000 ms, that is 5 seconds. In total about 5 + 5 = 10 seconds. The real start of the alarm can be late by up to the quarter-second check interval; that is why there is a small margin.

quiz.prompt: The same circuit has an RTC (DS3231) and an MPU6050, both at their default addresses. What happens?
options: No problem; I2C tells each device apart automatically
Only the RTC works, the MPU6050 breaks
quiz.explanation: On I2C, devices are chosen by address. If both use 0x68, there is no telling which one will answer. The fix: as in this course, do not use the two in the same circuit, or change the MPU6050's address (0x69 with the AD0 pin).
